metadata.title: Nasal Air‐Jet Sensitivity Differentiates Empty Nose Syndrome and Turbinate Reduction Patients: A Pilot Study

sections.text: ABSTRACT Objectives Abnormal nasal mucosal function has been frequently implicated in the symptomatology of empty nose syndrome (ENS), yet with limited evidence. This prospective pilot study aims to compare nasal mucosal sensitivity to air‐jet stimuli between ENS patients and patients who underwent septoplasty/turbinate reduction (septo‐turb) surgery, but without ENS symptoms. Methods Seven ENS and seven septo‐turb subjects were recruited through a sample of convenience (from 06/2023 to 09/2024) due to the rarity of ENS. A precise, 0.25 s air jet ranging from 0.5 to 5 L/min was delivered via a 25‐gage microcannula, with a 0.4 × 1.6 mm side opening placed 2 mm from the mucosal surface at predetermined sites that include the medial and lateral side of the nasal valve, the head and the center of inferior turbinate and their opposing septum. Detection thresholds were determined using a single‐staircase method in 0.5 L/min steps. Results The ENS group had a significantly higher (less sensitive) threshold than the septo‐turb group for the septum opposing the center of the inferior turbinate (ENS: 2.43 ± 1.37 L/min; septoplasty: 1.39 ± 1.27 L/min, p = 0.016); however, not for other sites. This regional threshold significantly correlated with all self‐reported symptom scores (NOSE, SNOT‐22, ENS6Q, VAS) ( r = 0.45–0.54, all p < 0.05). Conclusion Significant regional differences in air‐jet stimulus sensitivity between ENS and septoplasty patients were found that significantly correlated with symptom scores. A future larger sample size would make a more definitive conclusion. Level of Evidence 3

Empty Nose Syndrome (ENS) is a rare and controversial complication of aggressive nasal airway surgery that is characterized by a paradoxical feeling of severe nasal obstruction despite seemingly adequate airflow through a patent nasal airway. Patients with ENS report persistent feelings of dyspnea, nasal pain, suffocation, air hunger, breathlessness, nasal dryness, and crusting [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. These symptoms can be severe and debilitating, creating a significant clinical challenge [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Turbinate hypertrophy and septal deviation are often co‐occurring causes of nasal obstruction [ 4 ] and thus are frequently corrected concurrently with turbinate reduction and/or septoplasty surgeries to alleviate obstructive symptoms and improve nasal airflow [ 5 ]. Although rare, extensive turbinate reduction surgeries can lead to complications including but not limited to crusting, dryness, postsurgical bleeding, and in extreme cases, ENS [ 6 , 7 ]. The perception of nasal obstruction is a complex interplay of nasal anatomy, airflow dynamics, and sensory stimulation [ 8 ]. As a result, subjective patient experience of nasal obstructive symptoms does not always correlate with objective measures of physical obstruction [ 9 , 10 ]. The exact mechanisms behind the symptomatology of nasal obstruction and the unexpected consequence of nasal surgery serving to correct them (ENS) have not yet been fully elucidated. Studies have suggested that ENS severity may be related to postsurgical inferior turbinate volume and morphology due to changes in anatomical structure resulting in perturbation of nasal airflow [ 11 ]. However, others suggest that pure anatomical explanations fall short of explaining the pathophysiology of ENS, with studies showing that the degree of reduction in inferior turbinate volume does not predict ENS occurrence [ 12 ] or even that ENS symptoms may be worse with increased remaining inferior turbinate volume [ 13 ]. Additional studies using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) modeling have demonstrated that ENS patients show differential patterns of nasal airflow, with jet‐stream patterns to the middle turbinate/meatus and lower resistance to airflow being common findings among ENS patients when compared to healthy controls [ 14 , 15 , 16 ]. One of the proposed mechanisms for this discrepancy is differential patterns of sensitivity to airflow of the trigeminal nerve, which provides somatosensory innervation to the nasal cavity via its ophthalmic and maxillary divisions [ 17 ]. Cool thermoreceptors of the trigeminal nerve, called TRPM8, play a critical role in the sensation of normal nasal airflow and feelings of nasal patency [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ]. As a result, defects in this receptor pathway have been investigated as a potential contributor to the symptomology of ENS [ 22 ]. Several studies have shown that patients with ENS perform significantly worse on menthol lateralization tests, which measure the functioning trigeminal TRPM8 cool pathway, when compared to patients without ENS [ 14 , 15 , 19 , 20 , 21 ]. Given this apparent relationship between ENS symptomology and trigeminal nerve functioning, this project aims to evaluate nasal mucosal sensitivity to mechanical air‐jet stimulation as an objective tool of evaluating nasal obstruction symptoms in patients with and without ENS following septoplasty and turbinate reduction surgery. We anticipate that patients with ENS would show lower sensitivity to airflow overall and at critical regions within the nasal mucosa, and that this lack of sensitivity would correlate with higher ratings of subjective symptoms.

Participants, 18 years or older, with a history of turbinate reduction and/or septoplasty who reported good outcomes and participants who reported Empty Nose Syndrome (ENS) were recruited. Participant enrollment was based on both physicians' diagnosis and patient self‐reported symptoms. Screening for medical and occupational history was accomplished through chart review. Participants with cystic fibrosis, Wegener's or any other connective tissue disorder, or head trauma were excluded from the study. Due to the rarity of ENS and the requirement of in‐person testing, we have to rely on ENS patients all across the United States and over the world to willingly travel to Columbus, Ohio on their own means, thus the sample size reflects our full recruiting efforts (from 06/2023 to 09/2024) and a sample of convenience rather than based on power calculation.

The nasal stimulation device (NSD) was constructed with three major components: a 1‐gal compressed air reservoir tank, a mass flow controller (Sensirion SFC‐5400), and a disposable 25G blunt‐tipped micro‐cannula, which is 2 in. long, 0.51 mm in diameter, with a side opening that is approximately 0.4 × 1.6 mm (Figure 1 ). Airtight connection between components was achieved through compression fittings. The mass flow controller was connected and controlled via external computer using proprietary software. Custom eyeglass frames were 3D printed to serve as a facial rig to lock the cannula assembly in place once placed in the correct orientation into the nasal cavity (Figure 1 ). This is to ensure stability of the cannula and to prevent movement during testing. Two versions of the frames were created, one for each nostril. Headphones were provided for the patient and white noise was delivered to prevent the patient from hearing the faint sound of the flow valve opening. This instrumentation is comparable to the air‐jet delivery systems used in previous studies among a healthy population [ 23 , 24 ].

The inferior turbinate was identified for each patient through nasal speculum, and the distance required for the cannula tip to reach the head of the inferior turbinate (IT) was marked, as well as a position 2 cm posterior from the IT head, which was marked as the center of the inferior turbinate as the IT is on average 5 cm long [ 25 ]. The cannula side port was placed at the medial and lateral side of the nasal valve, the inferior turbinate head and its opposing septum, and the center of the inferior turbinate and its opposing septum (Figure 2 ). These locations were chosen based on previous studies looking at a healthy population [ 23 , 24 ], as well as the functional importance of the nasal valve and inferior turbinate [ 26 , 27 ]. Middle turbinate sites were omitted as participant discomfort made accurate placement of the cannula difficult. The cannula port was placed at the desired location and approximately 2 mm to the mucosal wall by a trained resident or medical student through visual inspection through nasal speculum and then subsequently locked in place by a facial rig that prevented the cannula from moving/rotating. Through pretesting training, the 2 mm is approximated based on visual landmarks and the diameter of the cannula. The cannula was double‐checked to not touch the nasal mucosa anywhere through visual inspection. These stimulations were performed for one nostril and then repeated for the other side. Air stimulations of 0.25 s duration were delivered in the 0.5 to 5 standard liters per minute (slm) range, with airflow speed calculated to be 13 to 130 m/s exiting the cannula opening. Air‐jet temperature was set to room temperature at 20°C–25°C. Air was pumped into the apparatus well in advance of the patient testing session and was allowed to reach equilibrium with room temperature. Starting from the lowest flow rate, a set of three stimuli was given for each rate and increased in steps of 0.5 slm. Two of the stimuli were blank with no airflow, with only one positive air flow stimulus. The subject was asked to identify which of the three stimuli was positive. Testing ended when the subject: (1) had responded correctly in two consecutive trials and (2) was certain that the last response was correct (equal or above 7 on a scale of 0–10 in confidence rating). The latter criterion represented an attempt to reduce the chances of a false positive, as two consecutive “lucky guesses” are not a rare event (11%). The stimulus threshold was determined as the first of the two consecutive correct trials [ 28 ]. This threshold testing was done on all testing sites, proceeding from the posterior to anterior direction, and testing was completed unilaterally for left and right side of the nasal cavity. The patient was instructed to breathe through the mouth during stimulation onset. This instrumentation and the testing protocol have been used in previous studies on healthy populations [ 23 , 24 ], where good test–retest reliability was reported [ 23 ].

Nasal symptoms were assessed for all participants using these peer‐reviewed questionnaires: Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation (NOSE) [ 29 ], Sino‐nasal Outcome Test (SNOT‐22) [ 30 ], Visual Analog Scale for Nasal Obstruction (VAS) where 0 was completely clear and 10 was completely obstructed, and Empty Nose Syndrome 6‐Item Questionnaire (ENS6Q) [ 31 ].

To determine the difference of nasal stimulation thresholds between the ENS and septoplasty groups, the nonparametric Wilcoxon Ranked Sum Test was used for all stimulation sites and symptom scores. For comparison of left and right nasal cavities, the Wilcoxon Signed‐Rank Test was used to determine if there were differences in thresholds. To determine the effect of stimulation location (nasal valve, center of the inferior turbinate, inferior turbinate head) and stimulation side (lateral wall vs. opposing septum) on stimulation thresholds, the nonparametric Kruskal–Wallis test was performed, with a post hoc Dunn's test. p ‐values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Nonparametric Spearman statistics were utilized for correlation analysis, with an alpha level of 0.05. These correlations were calculated between the stimulation thresholds and the different self‐reported symptom scores. Using the same nonparametric methods, correlations were also made for the time interval between surgery and follow‐up appointment and the different self‐reported symptom scores.

Seven ENS patients (two women and five men; age = 36 ± 9 years) and seven septo‐turb patients (three women and four men; age = 40 ± 20 years) were recruited for the study. All ENS patients had undergone bilateral inferior turbinate resection/reduction in the past, with four patients who underwent additional septal deviation repair, and one patient with surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE) and an endoscopic middle meatal antrostomy. All matched septo‐turb patients underwent bilateral inferior turbinate reduction/resection on top of the septoplasty, with three patients receiving additional maxillary antrostomy. All septo‐turb patients were scheduled at a minimum of 2 months from their surgery date, but this follow‐up time obviously varies greatly, especially among the ENS group. In response, we collected intervals between surgery and testing date for both septo‐turb and ENS patients and examined the correlation between this interval and symptoms. The demographic characteristics of the patients and their self‐reported nasal symptom scores are shown in Table 1 . There was no significant difference in age between the ENS and septo‐turb groups ( p > 0.05). The septo‐turb patients had significantly lower symptom scores, as compared to the ENS patients (NOSE, SNOT‐22, VAS, ENS6Q, all p < 0.05).

There was a significant difference in stimulation threshold between ENS and septo‐turb patients at the opposing septum of the center of the inferior turbinate ( Wilcoxon Ranked Sum Test Statistic (W) = 150, p = 0.016), with a higher (less sensitive) mean for the ENS group (M = 2.43 L/min, SD = 1.37) than the septo‐turb group (M = 1.39 L/min, SD = 1.27) (Figure 2 ). Thresholds at other stimulation sites were not significantly different between the two groups (Table 1 ). For the ENS group, there was a significant difference in stimulation threshold between the different locations ( χ 2 (2) = 8.748, p = 0.013), with significantly lower threshold for the nasal valve when compared to the inferior turbinate head ( z = −1.958, p = 0.05) and the center of the inferior turbinate ( z = −2.899, p = 0.004) after the post hoc Dunn's test. The side of each location (lateral wall or opposing septum) did not show any significance, and there was no significant difference between the inferior turbinate head and the center of the inferior turbinate for the ENS group. For the septo‐turb group, there were no significant differences between the locations and side of location pairs (lateral wall or opposing septum). See Table 2 for the comparative statistics for the ENS and septo‐turb groups. There was no significant difference between left and right nasal cavity thresholds for both the ENS and septo‐turb groups ( p > 0.05) (Table 2 ).

sections.section: Correlations Between Nasal Stimulation Thresholds And Self‐Reported Nasal Symptom Scores
sections.text: Significant correlations were found between the stimulation threshold at the opposing septum of the center of the inferior turbinate and the SNOT score ( r = 0.54, p < 0.05), the VAS score ( r = 0.45, p < 0.05), the NOSE score ( r = 0.44, p < 0.05), and the ENS6Q score ( r = 0.52, p < 0.05) (Table 3 ). These correlations were all positive, indicating worse (higher) stimulation thresholds are associated with worse (higher) symptom scores (Figure 3 ). For other locations : There was no significant correlation between the self‐reported nasal symptom scores and stimulation thresholds at other stimulation sites for both ENS and septo‐turb (all p > 0.05). Additionally, no significant correlation was found between the time interval from surgery to follow‐up and self‐reported nasal symptom scores among both the septo/turb and ENS group (all p > 0.05), except the NOSE scores for the ENS group ( ρ = −0.786, p < 0.001). The negative correlation indicates that the longer the interval, the better NOSE score among the ENS group, which may reflect adapting to the symptoms. However, no such trends were found for the other symptom scores.

In this study we were investigating the difference in nasal trigeminal sensitivity to airflow stimuli between ENS patients and postoperative septo‐turb patients. Using a custom‐built device that could deliver precise volumes and speed of air stimulus consistently, we measured the sensitivity thresholds of six different sites in the nasal valve and the inferior turbinate and found a significant difference in regional sensitivity between the two population groups only for the septum opposing the center of the inferior turbinate. Significant positive correlations were found between the self‐reported nasal symptom scores and the regional stimulation threshold, demonstrating that nasal symptoms could be tied with lower regional mucosal sensitivity to airflow stimulation. Previous studies have repeatedly shown that the nasal valve/vestibule has the greatest degree of sensitivity to airflow stimuli among a healthy population [ 23 , 24 , 32 ]. It is also expected for there to be a gradation in threshold sensitivity as we go from the posterior to anterior regions of the nasal cavity [ 24 , 32 ]. While our findings were in line with previous studies with the ENS group, the septo‐turb group appeared to contradict previous studies, which is puzzling as postsurgical septo‐turb patients with good outcomes would be expected to be most in line with a healthy population. But these patients are not healthy controls, and all have undergone turbinate reduction surgeries that may impact mucosal sensitivities. Further investigation into a larger sample size will be required to fully assess this contradictory result. Another interesting result from this study is the significant differentiation between the ENS and septo‐turb populations only at the septum opposing the center of the inferior turbinate but not at other sites. The inferior turbinate has been frequently implicated in ENS pathology [ 11 ]. However, previous studies have shown that there is a paradoxical difference in nasal patency when comparing ENS patients with other patient groups that have had comparable inferior turbinate reduction/resections [ 12 ]. As ENS patients and septo‐turb patients often both undergo inferior turbinate modification, the decrease in airflow sensitivity could be attributed to trauma to the IT mucosal lining. However, paradoxically, the septum opposing the center of the inferior turbinate in the current study showed a more profound decrease in sensitivity in ENS patients when compared to the septo‐turb group. Potential speculations are that ENS patients could have had more disruption/trauma to the septum postsurgery or have a lower baseline sensitivity prior to surgery as compared to septo‐turb patients, leading to diminished sensation of airflow and the distinction between the two patient groups. With thermoreceptors being credited for a larger role in nasal patency through detecting temperature changes, the role or existence of mechanoreceptors in the sense of breathing remains unclear [ 33 , 34 ]. Room temperature airflow passing over the mucosa will cool the tissue through evaporative and conductive convection; it is possible the participants were experiencing a cooling stimulus in addition to a mechanical stimulus. Some participants did report that during testing they were distinguishing the airflow stimulus based on the cooling sensation. Previous studies investigating nasal patency have stressed the importance of mucosal cooling sensation in feelings of nasal obstruction, and disruption to these receptors could result in diminished sensation. Additionally, while there have been many studies [ 33 ], the role of other potential receptors beyond thermal sensing TRPs in human temperature sensation is unclear in current literature. Studies looking into the topographical distribution of thermal receptors across the nasal cavity have been done mostly in rodents [ 35 ]. One such previous study has shown that there is a large concentration of calcitonin gene‐related peptide (CGRP) immunoreactive nerve fibers at the septal mucosa as compared to the lateral wall and other regions in the nasal cavity [ 36 ]. Perhaps there are parallels in nasal physiology from rodent to human nasal physiology that could explain the role of the nasal septum in airflow sensation; however, this is speculative. This study has limitations that should be acknowledged. First off, the sample size of both populations is limited due to the pilot nature of the study as well as the rarity of ENS. Additionally, testing of additional sites such as the middle turbinate was not done due to participant discomfort and limitations of the medical student skill set. Finally, the effect of time interval from surgery to follow‐up appointment for the ENS group (specifically NOSE score) could have served as a confounding factor. Due to these limitations, the findings should be interpreted with caution. Future studies should expand to include a larger sample size as well as more sites along the nasal cavity.

In our pilot study, the preliminary results suggest significant regional differences in the nasal mucosal sensitivity between ENS and septo‐turb patients that significantly correlated with self‐reported nasal symptom scores. These regional differences may play an important role in the sensation of breathing for patients with sinonasal disorders. Further expansion of the study is required to fully assess and understand the perception of nasal airflow among different disease populations.
